data.title: GOP lawmakers bash Trump's decision to waive Russia sanctions: 'Beyond irresponsible'
data.description:
Several GOP lawmakers criticized President Trump’s move to exempt Russia from the sanctions bill he signed law last month, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R- N.C.) calling the move “Beyond irresponsible.”

Trump signed an executive order Friday evening to waive sanctions against Russia in a legislative package that was meant to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its military operations against Ukraine.

“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis wrote on the social platform X.

The legislation, signed by Trump in September, would impose tariffs on the top five purchasers of Russian energy, or on countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

The sanctions bill was drafted by and named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The late senator had announced a breakthrough on the legislation shortly before his death in July, saying lawmakers reached a deal with the White House to move it forward.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) posted the news on social media Saturday morning saying, “Lindsey would be appalled.”

“The President is prolonging the war, not ending it,” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) wrote on social media, referring to Friday’s executive order.  

In his Friday order, the president noted that the legislation allows him to “waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person.”

“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump said in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”

One the other side of the aisle, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who played a major role in passing the sanctions bill, called the president’s move to waive sanctions for Russia, a “craven, cowardly action.”

“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal wrote in his post.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) also slammed the president’s move on social platform X, saying it “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression.”

The move comes after the president struck a deal with Russia last week permitting the country to sell diesel products to the U.S. and in the world market amid global fuel shortages. The deal prompted backlash from lawmakers across the board.

In an interview with Piers Morgan, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt “betrayed” by the president’s decision.

data.title: Corrections costs keep rising — but are we buying safer communities?
data.description:
A prison sentence ends on a particular day. The public’s stake in what happens next does not. 

Former inmates, released and coming home, must find work, meet supervision requirements and live without harming anyone else. Whether prison prepared them matters to everyone in the community receiving them. 

The Justice Department has estimated that approximately 95 percent of incarcerated people will eventually be released. Taxpayers should expect corrections to prepare them for that return. 

States spent an estimated $80.4 billion on corrections in fiscal 2025, up from $74.5 billion two years earlier. Those figures include capital spending and are not adjusted for inflation. 

Pennsylvania shows what that pressure looks like. Its average cost per incarcerated person rose from $169.71 to $197.63 per day over five fiscal years. The department says the increase largely tracked inflation as the custodial population remained relatively stable in recent years.

But rising costs do not guarantee larger budgets. Texas leaders recently directed state agencies to reduce their base budget requests by 3 percent for the 2028-2029 period. Corrections leaders still have to maintain security, support officers and prepare people for release. Governors should give them the authority to improve operations and reward better performance. Savings that leave more victims behind are no bargain.

A budget cannot capture the fear of returning to work, the loss of a livelihood or the absence of someone who will never come home. And when another crime follows release, the greatest cost falls on the victim.

Preventing that harm belongs at the center of how we judge corrections.

I saw what better operations could mean while leading a facility holding people from four jurisdictions whose populations had to remain separate. We listened to both staff and incarcerated people, improved routines and made expectations clearer. Turnover fell so low that we went three years without needing a new academy.

That experience taught me that working conditions and leadership belong in the budget conversation.

Today, the national Safe Inside project reports more than $2 billion in correctional overtime spending in 2024, nearly twice the amount in 2019. A system struggling to keep its staff needs more than another recruiting campaign.

Governors should reward correctional leaders and facility teams for safer prisons, stronger staff retention and lower recidivism after release. Set clear expectations and let facilities share in the benefits of their success.

Arizona offers a practical example. After it adopted probation reforms emphasizing incentives and evidence-based supervision, new felony convictions among probationers fell by 31 percent over two years. Today, state law ties probation incentive funding to reduced prison admissions, supporting treatment, training and officer recognition. The lesson for prison leadership: Make public safety the goal, measure progress and reward verified success.

Governors and legislators should make this a statewide requirement. The next corrections budget should require every facility to have a funded improvement plan, measurable targets and authority over defined spending decisions within 12 months — and report progress publicly each year.

Three changes would put that commitment into practice. First, make preparation part of the sentence. Assess literacy, work skills and treatment needs at intake. Set expectations for conduct and participation. Before lawful release, verify identification, housing arrangements, necessary treatment appointments and connections to supervision and employment services. Put someone in charge of making that transition happen.

Second, measure performance fairly. Report violence, staff retention, overtime and release preparation in correctional facilities. Track employment and new offenses afterward, distinguishing crimes from supervision violations. Independent evaluators should compare similar populations and account for risk and transfers. Wardens cannot control every decision after release, but they can answer for preparation. Governors remain responsible for adequate resources and services across the system.

Third, give wardens and their teams a defined operating budget, financial training and authority to manage it. Monthly reports should show spending, what drives overtime and which costs they can control. Central offices should retain audits, statewide purchasing and safety requirements while allowing approved local decisions.

Make verified improvement count toward promotions and authorized team awards. Allow facilities to carry forward an approved share of demonstrated savings for staff development and effective programs. Require corrective action when results fall short. Cutting necessary care, leaving security posts unfilled or hiding incidents must never qualify as success.

Secure confinement remains necessary for dangerous people. Preparing people for lawful release protects the public without excusing crime or promising everyone will change.

Recognizing the possibility of change asks nothing of a victim’s forgiveness. It places a demand on the person who caused the harm. Take responsibility. Develop useful skills. Meet your obligations. Stop creating victims.

Taxpayers should ask their governors to put these expectations into the next budget. Rising costs may finally get our attention. The next potential victim is why we must act.

Brian Koehn is a former warden and founder and CEO of Social Purpose Corrections, a nonprofit focused on corrections and reentry.

data.title: Live updates: Trump and Zelensky relationship rocky over Russia sanctions, Starlink; Obama campaigns in Michigan, Ohio
data.description:
President Trump is set to travel back and forth between Mar a Lago and Highland Heights, Kentucky on Saturday, where he is set to deliver remarks at 2 p.m., but former President Barack Obama will also be holding campaign events in Ohio and Michigan.

The former Democratic president will travel to Detroit and Cleveland in an attempt to move the needle in the two midwestern swing states.

Michigan is home to highly competitive gubernatorial, Senate and House races, as the state’s Senate race between Abdul El-Sayed (D) and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) has been in the national spotlight.

Trump announced he will be campaigning in the Wolverine State on Oct. 25, while Vice President Vance campaigned with Rogers earlier this week. Trump is set to make additional stops in Wichita, Kan., Greenville, N.C., Clemson, S.C., Sioux City, Iowa, Fort Myers, Fla. and Macon, Ga. next week.

Outside of the midterms, Trump announced Friday that the U.S. would waive sanctions against Russia set to take effect soon under a recently signed legislative package. The president signed the sanctions package into law last month, which was posthumously dedicated to the late Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-S.C.). 

The move follows Trump’s decision to strike a deal with Russia last week to permit the country to sell diesel products to the U.S., and after Ukraine reported a Starlink outage this week that impacted their air defense operations.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has escalated the Starlink matter, accusing the Trump administration of throttling its access to the satellite system and failing to offer standard intelligence on incoming Russian strikes.

On Friday, Trump said neither he nor Musk caused the outage, saying, “we didn’t do that at all. In fact, I don’t even think it was slowed down from what I understood.”

Follow live below.

data.title: Trader Joe's to open more than 30 new stores 'soon': Here's where
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – After consulting its “maps and compass,” Trader Joe’s has announced plans to expand in multiple cities, marking just the latest expected expansion of the nation’s favorite grocer.

Trader Joe’s previously confirmed it would open at least 25 stores this year. The latest of those new stores recently opened in Herriman, Utah, and Lafayette, Louisiana, according to the company’s website. A store in Reading, Massachusetts, celebrated its grand opening on Wednesday.

Last week, the grocer shared the next three cities in which it expects to open new locations: 

  • Bend, Oregon: 61284 S. Highway 97
  • Boynton Beach, Florida: 334 N Congress Ave Unit B
  • Phoenix, Arizona: 4519 East Thomas Road

Trader Joe’s expects to open all three in 2027. 

This will be Boynton Beach’s first such store, while Bend and Phoenix are already home to one Trader Joe’s store each. Phoenix is, however, on track to see another location open “soon,” according to the grocer’s website. 

Here’s where Trader Joe’s anticipates opening other new stores “soon,” as of Oct. 12: 

  • Arizona: Phoenix (21001 North Tatum Boulevard, Suite 1030)
  • California: Anaheim Hills (6336 East Santa Ana Canyon Road), Leucadia (1590 Leucadia Boulevard), Riverbank (2135 Claribel Road), San Diego (3962 Clairemont Mesa Boulevard)
  • Colorado: Denver (8564 East Northfield Boulevard)
  • Florida: Orlando (1444 North Alafaya Trail) and Sarasota (8199 S Tamiami Trail Unit 100)
  • Illinois: Oswego (1930 US-34), Chicago (804 West Montrose Avenue and 6191 N. Lincoln Avenue), Joliet (2741 Plainfield Road)
  • Maryland: Baltimore (6311 York Road – Anneslie)
  • Massachusetts: Quincy (111 General McConville Way)
  • Michigan: Farmington Hills (27658 Middlebelt Road)
  • Nebraska: Omaha (192nd and Burke Street)
  • New Jersey: West Orange (471 Mt. Pleasant Avenue) and Jersey City (55 Hudson Street)
  • New York: Syracuse (3515 West Genesee Street) and Yonkers (2482 Central Park Avenue)
  • Ohio: University Heights (2643 Warrensville Center Road)
  • Texas: Bellaire (5130 Bellaire Boulevard Suite 100), Cedar Park (1800 East Whitestone Boulevard), and Mansfield (1580 East Debbie Lane)
  • Utah: West Jordan (5561 W 7800 S)
  • Washington: Seattle (401 NE Northgate Way) and Spokane Valley (13414 East Sprague Avenue)

While there is no designated opening date for these locations, a Trader Joe’s spokesperson previously confirmed to Nexstar that stores are typically marked as “opening soon” online three to six months before they’re expected to open. 

Trader Joe’s lists openings at several of the above locations, potentially indicating plans to open sooner rather than later. That includes at stores opening in Baltimore, Chicago, Jersey City, Phoenix, Quincy, Reading, Riverbank, San Diego, Spokane Valley, and Syracuse. Starting pay for the positions, which are primarily “crew” with a few “mate” managerial roles, ranges from $16 to $32 an hour. 

Officials in Oswego, Joliet, Riverbank, Spokane Valley, and University Heights suggested their new Trader Joe’s stores could open yet this fall. The new New York locations could open before the year ends. Trader Joe’s previously reported that it planned to open its store in Reading in 2026. 

As of late 2026, you can find the nautical-themed retailer in 42 states and the District of Columbia. The only states still awaiting a Trader Joe’s store are Alaska, Hawaii, Mississippi, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, West Virginia, and Wyoming.

data.title: Trump administration says painting Eisenhower building would hurt landmark's history
data.description:
The Trump administration’s plan to put a coat of white paint on the exterior of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building would diminish the historic character of the 19th-century landmark, according to a draft environmental assessment published Friday.

“The unpainted exterior granite walls, including their natural detail (e.g., grey and pink hues), were hand-selected by the architect and are central to the building’s historic character and original design intent,” the assessment read.

The administration’s proposal to paint the Eisenhower building is a part of President Trump’s larger plan of beautifying the nation’s capital. The exterior paint job is estimated to cost at least $7.5 billion.

The proposal alarmed preservationists, architects, historians and others who argue that granite is not meant to be painted and that paint would trap moisture and deteriorate the stone.

Friday’s report found that the proposed white mineral silica paint is weather resistant and permeable enough that it is unlikely for moisture to be trapped beneath the surface, according to the assessment report.

“Mineral silicate paints are advertised as highly breathable and durable wall coatings that are composed of natural minerals and potassium silicate,” the report noted.

In August, a federal judge allowed the administration to conduct paint tests on the 19th-century building after finding that concerns raised by preservation groups did not prove the testing could cause “irreparable harm.” The judge said the ruling applied only to testing and not the entire project.

Trump has previously criticized the building’s appearance, saying last year that its gray exterior is a “really bad color.”

The Eisenhower building sits next door to the White House and was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1969. It was also listed on the National Register of Historic Places and the District of Columbia Inventory of Historic Sites in 1972.

data.title: The Memo: Ukraine's slide into crisis sharpens questions for Trump
data.description:
Tumult and doubt are hanging over the role of the United States in the war in Ukraine, 4 1/2 years after the Russian invasion.

That’s the bottom line after a week of high drama that roiled Washington, Kyiv and concerned political leaders in Europe.

The U.S. stance is, of course, determined by President Trump, often in unpredictable fashion.

On Friday, he denied to reporters that either he or his sometime ally Elon Musk had decided to restrict Ukrainian usage of the Starshield satellite system, which is vital to the effectiveness of Kyiv’s drones.

“I didn’t do that. No, we didn’t do that at all. In fact, I don’t even think it was slowed down from what I understood. Because I just checked this morning,” Trump told reporters Friday as he left the White House en route to a campaign rally in Georgia.

The Ukrainians are adamant that the system was indeed slowed down — one of several developments about which they are incensed, blaming the U.S. for having undermined a war effort that they have fought against the odds and at enormous cost.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told a Friday news conference in Brussels that the initial slowing down of the Starshield system had come as “a dangerous and unpleasant surprise,” according to The Associated Press.

Zelensky also disputed the idea that the system had been restored to normal function.

“Have they returned to previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back? Yes,” he said.

The Starshield issue was perhaps the most shocking episode in a recent chapter of drama and recrimination between Kyiv and the White House.

Trump’s Oct. 9 announcement of a deal for Russian diesel caused widespread consternation, given its capacity to ease economic pressure on Moscow. Zelensky and his allies had been seeking to ramp up this pressure. In Washington, Congress recently passed legislation, in memory of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), intensifying sanctions against Moscow.

Trump’s assertion that there was an “Energy Ceasefire” between the warring parties has come to seem hollow.

Russia never appeared to accede to the idea of a mutual pause on hitting infrastructure facilities, and Ukraine duly abandoned its willingness to hold off striking Russian refineries.

There have also been conflicting reports about whether the United States was withholding intelligence from Ukraine, which Trump has denied.

Recent days have been interspersed with heated words.

Trump has suggested Ukraine should replace Zelensky as its president. In an interview with Newsmax, broadcast Thursday evening, Trump complained that Zelensky is “not a good guy for us to deal with” and also appeared to blame the Ukrainian president, at least in part, for having “destroyed that country.” 

Zelensky, for his part, this week told British journalist Piers Morgan that he felt his nation had been betrayed, in part by the diesel deal. He also told Morgan that he regretted that Ukraine was “losing” the U.S. as a strong partner.

Amid all the bleakness, it looks as if U.S.-Ukraine relations are at their lowest ebb since the infamous February 2025 Oval Office meeting at which Zelensky was berated by Trump and Vice President Vance.

The effects on the battlefield are plain to see.

According to the AP, the latest spate of Russian attacks hit at least nine areas of Ukraine, leaving “hundreds of thousands of households” without power. Those attacks will bite with special fierceness as winter sets in across eastern Europe.

Trump, pinioned by rising gas prices stemming from the war on Iran that he launched in conjunction with Israel earlier this year, appears to be trying to shift blame to Ukraine for pain at American pumps.

His social media message announcing the diesel deal said that the new arrangement — as well as what he inaccurately termed American “TOTAL CONTROL” of the Strait of Hormuz — would mean that “Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!”

According to AAA, the average U.S. diesel price Friday was approximately $6.33, up from $6.28 on the day Trump announced the Russia deal — and hugely increased from the $3.65 level at which it stood one year ago.

Rick Tyler, a Republican strategist who is often critical of Trump, complained that the diesel deal amounted to “amateur hour.”

“It won’t work, and yet people are going to think we are going to get lower gas prices,” Tyler told this column.

He also blasted Trump’s general approach as “despicable” and said, regarding the president’s approach to Russian President Vladimir Putin, that Trump was “sacrificing the credibility of the United States when he engages with a thug like that who is killing innocent civilians.”

Meanwhile, confusion and controversy continue to swirl around the specifics of the Starlink matter.

On Thursday evening, Reuters reported that the order to limit the way the system could be used by Ukraine “came from inside the White House.” The news agency sourced that information to “two U.S. officials and a Western official.”

In addition to Trump’s Friday denial that either he or Musk was responsible, a U.S. official also told NewsNation, “No such request was ever made by the President.” (NewsNation and The Hill are both owned by Nexstar Media Group.)

Then, late Friday, The Telegraph reported that it was Musk who had “approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine.” Musk had previously implicitly denied he played any decisive role.

Meanwhile in Washington, four GOP senators joined with Democratic colleagues in seeking more information about the Pentagon’s role in the episode.

Whatever more is revealed about the specifics, there’s no mistaking the consternation felt by Republicans outside of Trump’s most fervent MAGA base about the current situation.

Doug Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee, contrasted Trump, very unfavorably, with the vigorous opposition to Moscow evinced by former President Reagan in the 1980s.

“It’s another 180, and it’s very depressing for anyone who considers themselves a traditional Republican,” Heye said.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

data.title: Ukraine faces grim question of whether it can take on Russia without US backing
data.description:
The disruptions this week in U.S. support for Ukraine have forced Kyiv to face a grim question: Can it stay in the fight against Russia without any of President Trump’s already diminished support?

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has escalated a diplomatic assault, earlier this week accusing the Trump administration of throttling its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite services and failing to offer standard intelligence on incoming Russian strikes. So far, U.S. weapons seem to still be flowing to Europe despite Trump’s turns in the war.

Uncertainty continues to swirl around who chose to limit SpaceX’s Starshield function, which has since been restored, but Reuters reported Thursday that the order to limit the satellite system came from inside the White House. Leaders at the Defense Department reportedly were told that the service needed to be slowed. 

Then on Friday, Trump said that neither he nor Musk caused the Starlink outage, telling reporters: “I didn’t do that. No, we didn’t do that at all.”

The episode highlights a growing rift between the U.S. and Ukraine, a dispute that puts Kyiv in danger and all but makes sure its war with Russia will stretch on for the foreseeable future, according to Branislav Slantchev, a political science professor at the University of California, San Diego.

“This hurts Ukraine in more ways than just limiting its ability to operate on the frontlines,” Slantchev said. 

He placed the blame squarely on the Pentagon for disrupting Ukraine’s Starlink and Starshield satellite services, with the former used for defensive purposes on the battlefield and the latter used for offensive operations. Starshield is controlled by the U.S. government and was slowed on Tuesday.  

He said the episode encourages Moscow to keep pushing with its demands including major territory concessions from Ukraine, as Russian President Vladimir Putin “estimates that the U.S. under Trump is on his side.” 

“Essentially, this guarantees that the war will continue,” Slantchev told The Hill. “Ukraine is not going to lose the war because of limited Starshield connectivity, but it makes Ukraine’s task of incapacitating Russia’s ability to hurt it much, much harder.”

Relations between Washington and Kyiv, already strained since Trump began his second term last year, were pushed to a new low last week after he announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian oil sales. The agreement allows diesel to enter the U.S. and global marketplace, giving Moscow a lifeline as it struggles to make gains on the battlefield.

Trump’s decision to allow the sales appeared influenced by the high cost of diesel in the United States, which has become an issue in congressional races, particularly in the Midwest. Yet there are doubts among experts of whether the step will reduce diesel’s costs given the connection between the high prices and turbulence in the Straight of Hormuz.

Zelensky has spoken out against the deal, saying he feels betrayed, criticism that Trump met with threats to cut off U.S. intelligence sharing.

Trump also demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries, saying Zelensky should be replaced as president. Trump has argued the Ukrainian attacks on the Russian infrastructure have contributed to rising fuel prices.

Washington insists it had not stopped intelligence sharing, but that was called into doubt on Tuesday after Ukraine noted the disruption in Starlink service after the country reportedly was not alerted by allies ahead of two Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv. The U.S. for more than four years has provided significant satellite and communications intelligence to Kyiv. 

Zelensky’s defense tech adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov, said that SpaceX without warning had introduced speed limits on its Starlink satellite internet terminals overnight, which “led to the failure of a number of missions.”

“It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” he said on Telegram.

Zelensky then said Wednesday that the slowdown of Starlink was a “big mistake” and warned that Ukrainians could die if speeds were not restored.

The Ukrainian leader also said that the U.S. is not “on the right side of history.

Trump until Friday had remained quiet on the mystery surrounding the Starlink service. Musk has said Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government, deflecting any involvement. 

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said in a post to X on Wednesday, referring to Trump. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”

Musk, who provided Starlink to Ukraine shortly after Russia invaded the country in February 2022, has turned off the satellite internet service in the past. In September 2022, as Ukraine was attempting to retake territory from Russia, Musk reportedly gave an order to turn off Starlink, putting Ukrainian troops in a communications blackout.

On Thursday the gloves seemed to come off for Kyiv after it reportedly said that it conducted a strike overnight against a Russian oil refinery.

Prior to that, Ukraine had said it would hold off on striking Kremlin energy targets at Trump’s request. But Moscow did not make a similar agreement and has continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure ahead of a brutally cold and dark winter.

data.title: Trump waives Russian sanctions outlined in Graham Act before they took effect
data.description:
President Trump signed an executive order Friday evening to waive sanctions against Russia set to take effect soon under a recently signed legislative package.

The president officially signed the sanctions package into law last month, which was posthumously dedicated to the late Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-S.C.). The legislation sought to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its yearslong military operations against Ukraine by imposing tariffs on top Russian energy purchasers and those who help the country evade sanctions.

The move comes as the Trump administration pushes efforts to lower fuel prices, which have risen amid the U.S.’s war in Iran.

Trump noted in his Friday order that the legislation allows him the ability to “waive the application of any sanctions provision” for foreign individuals.

“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” he said in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”

The move follows Trump’s decision to strike a deal with Russia last week to permit the country to sell diesel products to the U.S. and in the world market amid global fuel shortages.

Under this agreement, the president said Russia could “immediately” begin supplying 300,000 tons of diesel, an additional 500,000 tons in November and then one million tons “immediately thereafter.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky pushed back on the news, telling Piers Morgan in a Wednesday interview he felt “betrayed” by the president’s decision. 

“It’s more complicated than just my emotions or just my feelings,” he added. “Yes, it depends not on me. Our country has to survive.” 

The deal elicited bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill, with five Republican lawmakers joining their Democratic colleagues to denounce the relief.

“We urge the Administration to revoke this license and not issue further general licenses that reopen Russian energy transactions and restore revenue to the Kremlin’s war chest,” the lawmakers wrote in a Thursday letter to the Trump administration.

Updated at 10:51 p.m. EDT

data.title: Zacharia speaks out after White House press secretary exit: 'It was an honor'
data.description:
Katie Zacharia issued her first public statement Friday night after a White House official announced she’d be “transitioning out” of the press secretary post after just five days in the role.

In a post on the social media platform X, Zacharia praised President Trump’s leadership, saying, “It was an honor to work for him.”

“President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man,” she wrote in her post, which included a picture of herself and Trump in the Oval Office.

She continued, “I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to.”

Zacharia’s departure follows the president’s remarks to reporters on Friday that he had advised her to “reconsider” the position. The former political commentator has now logged the shortest press secretary tenure in the position’s history.

Her exit also followed a wave of scrutiny over a shaky debut press conference, which lasted 14 minutes and included only three questions from conservative-leaning outlets, as well as skepticism over her legal background. 

Zacharia, who replaced former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, had presented herself as a lawyer during her TV appearances. When asked by a reporter on Tuesday about which state she passed the bar exam in, Zacharia responded, “When I moved to China.”

However, the Wall Street Journal reported later that evening that she had failed the exam, prompting watchdog group Campaign for Accountability to file a complaint with the State Bar of California on Wednesday over her claims that she is a lawyer. 

In an interview with conservative outlet Real America’s Voice, Zacharia said she “misheard” the question but added that her bar exam results were “inconsequential” because she moved to China with her husband for work after graduation. 

Anthony Scaramucci, who served as White House communications director during Trump’s first term for 11 days, responded to Zacharia’s departure on Friday. 

“Records are made to be broken,” Scaramucci wrote on social media. “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”

data.title: Federal agents searched Omar's trash for DNA before raid: Sources
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Federal agents collected garbage in hopes of obtaining the DNA of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) and her family before this week’s raid at her Washington, D.C. home, sources told NewsNation.

Investigators historically have used secretive “dumpster diving” to obtain DNA when search warrants were not possible or would have tipped off investigatory targets. It is legally permissible for law enforcement to collect trash that has been discarded for pickup and comb through it for genetic material.

Multiple sources familiar with the probe tell NewsNation that potential DNA evidence is critical to the investigation into Omar. They say the case is broader than the public may assume based on longstanding accusations surrounding her immigration history or marital status.

The investigation encompasses family members of the congresswoman, with evidence expected to go before a grand jury, sources said. Relatives of the lawmaker have been named in some of the subpoenas issued by federal prosecutors, NewsNation reported.

Federal agents seized Omar’s phone during a widely publicized search Monday at her Washington residence. NewsNation has learned that more than a dozen raids actually occurred simultaneously.

The case is being coordinated within the Minneapolis office of Homeland Security Investigations, suggesting it may be related to public benefits fraud committed by some members of the Somali immigrant community in the region.

The 44-year-old Omar, who seeks a fifth term in Congress, was born in Somalia and immigrated to the U.S. as a child in 1995. She was naturalized in 2000.

She originally was investigated by the Department of Justice under former President Biden before the case was closed. Parts of that investigation were reopened and expanded under the administration of President Trump.

Omar, a frequent political foil for Trump, said she believes the DOJ has been weaponized against her. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Real America’s Voice Friday its case into the lawmaker is “about enforcing our nation’s laws.”
